subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
summary: Why atoms combine and what shape the result takes: Lewis structures and formal charge, ionic bonding and lattice enthalpy, bond parameters and resonance, VSEPR shapes, valence bond theory and hybridisation, molecular orbital theory for diatomic molecules, and hydrogen bonding. Every later chapter in organic, inorganic and coordination chemistry assumes this one.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 has no board exam. In the school final this chapter is typically one of the heaviest in the physical-chemistry part, with an MCQ or two, a short answer on shape or dipole moment and a long answer on hybridisation or molecular orbital theory. It is also the base for Class 12 boards (coordination compounds, organic mechanisms) and gets two to four questions a year in JEE and NEET.

question_types.note: Shape or hybridisation of a given species, bond order and magnetic nature from MOT, which molecule has zero dipole moment, which species does not exist.
Bond angle and lone-pair repulsion, bond order against bond length, dipole moment against symmetry, conductivity of ionic solids.
Draw a Lewis structure, calculate formal charge, state hybridisation and shape with reason, calculate bond order of a diatomic ion.
Explain a shape or bond-angle trend by VSEPR, compare sigma and pi bonds, explain why O<sub>2</sub> is paramagnetic, Fajans' rule.

Hybridisation of carbon in ethane, ethene and ethyne with orbital diagrams; MO diagram, bond order and magnetism of N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>; VSEPR treatment of PCl<sub>5</sub> or SF<sub>6</sub>.
A passage on hydrogen bonding, VSEPR shapes or MOT with four short sub-questions.

hot_topics: VSEPR shapes and bond angles of CH4, NH3, H2O, PCl5, SF6, ClF3, XeF2, XeF4
Hybridisation of carbon in ethane, ethene and ethyne, with the count of sigma and pi bonds
MO configuration, bond order and magnetic nature of N2, O2, O2+, O2-, O2 2-, He2
Formal charge and resonance in O3, CO3 2- and NO3-
Dipole moment: CO2 vs H2O, NH3 vs NF3, BeH2
Hydrogen bonding and boiling points (H2O vs H2S, o- vs p-nitrophenol)
Lattice enthalpy, factors favouring ionic bonding, Fajans' rule

sections.heading: 4.1 Kössel–Lewis Approach to Chemical Bonding
sections.body:
Kössel and Lewis (1916) explained bonding with the octet rule: atoms combine so that each ends up with eight electrons in its valence shell, the configuration of the nearest noble gas (hydrogen settles for a duplet of two). The octet can be reached by transferring electrons from one atom to another, giving ions that attract each other electrostatically (an electrovalent or ionic bond), or by sharing electron pairs between atoms (a covalent bond, Lewis's idea).

A Lewis symbol shows the valence electrons of an atom as dots around its symbol; the number of dots equals the group valence electrons, and the number needed to complete the octet is the usual valency. To draw a Lewis structure: add up the valence electrons of all atoms (add one for each negative charge, subtract one for each positive charge), put the least electronegative atom in the centre, join atoms with single bonds, complete the octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs, place any electrons left over on the central atom, and convert lone pairs into double or triple bonds if the central atom still lacks an octet.

Formal charge on an atom = (valence electrons in the free atom) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). In ozone the central O has formal charge 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, the doubly bonded O has 6 − 4 − 2 = 0 and the singly bonded O has 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Formal charge picks the best of several possible structures: the one with the smallest charges, and with negative charge on the more electronegative atom, is preferred.

Limitations of the octet rule, which examiners like: incomplete octets in LiCl, BeH2, BF3 and AlCl3; odd-electron molecules NO and NO2, which can never satisfy it; expanded octets in PF5, SF6 and H2SO4, where the central atom holds more than eight electrons; the rule says nothing about shape or bond energy; and it cannot explain why noble gases form compounds such as XeF2 and XeF4.

where: valence electrons of the free atom
non-bonding (lone pair) electrons on that atom in the structure
total bonding (shared) electrons around that atom

sections.tip: When two Lewis structures are both possible, show the formal-charge arithmetic for each and then choose. Asserting the answer without the numbers loses the method mark.

sections.heading: 4.2 Ionic or Electrovalent Bond
sections.body:
An ionic bond forms when a metal atom of low ionisation enthalpy loses electrons to a non-metal atom of high (very negative) electron gain enthalpy, and the cations and anions pack into a lattice held together by electrostatic attraction. NCERT's example is NaCl: Na(g) → Na+(g) + e− costs 495.8 kJ mol−1, and Cl(g) + e− → Cl−(g) releases only 348.7 kJ mol−1, so forming the free ions is endothermic. The compound is stable anyway because arranging the ions into the crystal releases 788 kJ mol−1, the lattice enthalpy, which more than covers the deficit.

NCERT defines lattice enthalpy as the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions; for NaCl, ΔlatticeH = +788 kJ mol−1. It rises with the charges on the ions and falls as the ions get bigger, so MgO, with 2+ and 2− ions, has a far larger lattice enthalpy than NaCl. The three favourable factors, in the wording the examiner expects: low ionisation enthalpy of the metal, high negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal, and high lattice enthalpy of the solid.

Ionic compounds are crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points, hard but brittle, insulators when solid but conductors when molten or dissolved because the ions become mobile, and soluble mainly in polar solvents such as water.

No bond is purely ionic. Fajans' rule (not spelt out in NCERT but asked in school exams): a small, highly charged cation polarises a large, easily deformable anion, pulling electron density into the region between the nuclei and giving the bond covalent character. This is why LiCl is more covalent than NaCl or KCl, and why AlCl3 behaves as a covalent compound.
sections.tip: Give the NCERT definition of lattice enthalpy (energy required to separate one mole of solid into gaseous ions) with its positive sign. The older 'energy released' wording is accepted only if you say it is the reverse process.

sections.heading: 4.3 Bond Parameters
sections.body:
Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, in picometres. Each atom contributes its covalent radius, so the length of A–B is rA + rB. It falls as bond order rises: C–C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm, C≡C 120 pm.

Bond angle is the angle between the orbitals holding the bonding pairs on a central atom, 104.5° for H–O–H in water; it fixes the shape of the molecule.

Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in the gaseous state. For a diatomic molecule it is the bond dissociation enthalpy: 435.8 kJ mol−1 for H–H, 498 kJ mol−1 for O=O. In a polyatomic molecule successive bonds cost different amounts: H2O(g) → H(g) + OH(g) needs 502 kJ mol−1 but OH(g) → H(g) + O(g) needs 427 kJ mol−1, so NCERT quotes the mean bond enthalpy, (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol−1 for O–H.

Bond order is the number of bonds between two atoms: 1 in H2, 2 in O2, 3 in N2. Isoelectronic species share a bond order (N2, CO and NO+ all have 3; F2 and O22− both have 1). As bond order rises, bond enthalpy rises and bond length falls.

Resonance: when a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, it is represented as a hybrid of two or more canonical structures that differ only in the positions of electrons. In O3 the two structures put the double bond on either O–O bond; the real molecule has two identical bonds of 128 pm, between a single (148 pm) and a double (121 pm) bond, and is more stable than any one canonical form (resonance stabilisation). CO32− and NO3− have three equivalent structures each.

Polarity: a bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar, with partial charges δ+ and δ−. The dipole moment μ = charge × distance is measured in debye (1 D = 3.33564 × 10−30 C m) and is a vector, drawn as an arrow from δ+ to δ−. In a polyatomic molecule the net dipole is the vector sum of the bond dipoles, so shape decides polarity: linear CO2 and trigonal planar BF3 have μ = 0 because their bond dipoles cancel, while bent H2O has μ = 1.85 D. In NH3 the lone-pair moment adds to the N–H dipoles (1.47 D); in NF3 it opposes the N–F dipoles (0.24 D).

where: dipole moment, in debye (D); 1 D = 3.33564 × 10<sup>−30</sup> C m
distance between the centres of positive and negative charge

formulas.expr: Mean bond enthalpy = (sum of successive bond dissociation enthalpies) / (number of bonds)

sections.tip: For 'CO2 has polar bonds but zero dipole moment', the marking point is the geometry: linear, the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. 'It is symmetrical' on its own is not enough.

sections.heading: 4.4 The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) Theory
sections.body:
VSEPR theory (Sidgwick and Powell, refined by Nyholm and Gillespie) predicts shape from the repulsion between electron pairs on the central atom. Postulates: the shape depends on the number of valence-shell electron pairs, bonding and non-bonding; the pairs stay as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion; a lone pair, held by one nucleus only, spreads out more than a bond pair, so repulsion decreases in the order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair; a multiple bond is treated as a single super pair; and lone pairs squeeze the angles between neighbouring bond pairs.

Shapes with no lone pairs: 2 pairs linear 180° (BeCl2, CO2); 3 pairs trigonal planar 120° (BF3); 4 pairs tetrahedral 109.5° (CH4); 5 pairs trigonal bipyramidal 120° and 90° (PCl5); 6 pairs octahedral 90° (SF6). With lone pairs (bp, lp): (2,1) bent, SO2; (3,1) trigonal pyramidal 107°, NH3; (2,2) bent 104.5°, H2O; (4,1) see-saw, SF4; (3,2) T-shaped, ClF3; (2,3) linear, XeF2; (5,1) square pyramidal, BrF5; (4,2) square planar, XeF4. In a trigonal bipyramid lone pairs always take equatorial positions, because there they suffer only two 90° repulsions instead of three; in an octahedron two lone pairs go opposite each other.

The standard question is the fall in bond angle from CH4 (109.5°) to NH3 (107°) to H2O (104.5°): each extra lone pair adds stronger lp–bp repulsion, and in water lp–lp repulsion as well, pushing the bond pairs closer together. Always name both the electron-pair geometry (tetrahedral for NH3) and the molecular shape (trigonal pyramidal).
sections.tip: Count lone pairs on the central atom before you name a shape. Water is bent, not linear, and the mark scheme checks the lone-pair count, the shape and the angle separately.

sections.heading: 4.5 Valence Bond Theory
sections.body:
Valence bond theory (Heitler and London, 1927, developed by Pauling) describes a covalent bond as the overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals. Take two hydrogen atoms far apart. As they approach, new forces appear: attraction between each nucleus and the other atom's electron, and repulsion between the two electrons and between the two nuclei. Attraction wins, the potential energy falls, and it reaches a minimum at an internuclear distance of 74 pm, the bond length of H2; the energy released, 435.8 kJ mol−1, is the bond enthalpy. Push the atoms closer and repulsion takes over, so the curve rises steeply. This energy–distance curve is a common diagram question.

Overlap can be positive (lobes of the same sign add and build electron density between the nuclei), negative (opposite signs cancel) or zero (an s orbital with a p orbital lying perpendicular to the axis). Only positive overlap bonds. Because p orbitals overlap best along their own axis, bonds have direction, which is why molecules have definite shapes.

A sigma (σ) bond comes from head-on overlap along the internuclear axis: s–s (H2), s–p (HCl), p–p end to end (Cl2). It is cylindrically symmetric about the axis and allows free rotation. A pi (π) bond comes from sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals perpendicular to the axis; the electron cloud sits above and below the axis, with a nodal plane through the nuclei, and rotation about the bond would break it. Sideways overlap is smaller than head-on overlap, so a π bond is weaker than a σ bond between the same atoms. A single bond is one σ, a double bond one σ + one π, a triple bond one σ + two π.
sections.tip: If asked to compare σ and π bonds for three marks, give three separate points: type of overlap, strength, and rotation about the bond. Add 'a π bond forms only after a σ bond exists' as a fourth.

sections.heading: 4.6 Hybridisation
sections.body:
Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy on the same atom to give the same number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals of identical energy and shape, pointing in fixed directions. The hybrid orbitals overlap more effectively than pure orbitals and so form stronger bonds. Orbitals need not be half-filled to hybridise: promotion of an electron (2s22p2 → 2s12p3 in carbon) is imagined first, and a hybrid orbital can hold a lone pair.

sp (one s + one p, two orbitals at 180°, linear): BeCl2; the carbons of ethyne, HC≡CH. Each carbon uses one sp orbital for the C–H σ bond and one for the C–C σ bond, and its two unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways with those of the other carbon to give two π bonds. Ethyne: 3 σ + 2 π, linear.

sp2 (one s + two p, three orbitals at 120°, planar): BF3; the carbons of ethene, H2C=CH2. Three sp2 orbitals form two C–H σ bonds and the C–C σ bond; the leftover p orbital on each carbon, perpendicular to the plane, forms the π bond. Ethene: 5 σ + 1 π, planar, C–C 134 pm.

sp3 (one s + three p, four orbitals at 109.5°, tetrahedral): CH4, ethane (7 σ, free rotation about C–C, 154 pm), NH3 (one hybrid holds the lone pair, 107°), H2O (two lone pairs, 104.5°).

sp3d (one s, three p, one d; trigonal bipyramidal): PCl5. Three equatorial P–Cl bonds lie in a plane at 120°; two axial bonds at 90° to it are slightly longer and weaker, because each axial pair suffers three 90° repulsions while an equatorial pair suffers only two. PCl5 is therefore reactive. sp3d2 (octahedral, 90°): SF6, all bonds equivalent.

Quick method: count σ bonds plus lone pairs on the central atom (the steric number): 2 sp, 3 sp2, 4 sp3, 5 sp3d, 6 sp3d2. So carbon in CH3–CHO is sp3 then sp2, and in BF3 + NH3 → F3B·NH3 boron changes from sp2 to sp3 while nitrogen stays sp3.

formulas.expr: Steric number = (σ bonds on the central atom) + (lone pairs on the central atom)
where: sp, sp<sup>2</sup>, sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>3</sup>d, sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> respectively

sections.tip: For ethane, ethene and ethyne, always write the hybridisation of each carbon and the σ/π count (7σ; 5σ + 1π; 3σ + 2π). Both items are on the marking scheme.

sections.heading: 4.7 Molecular Orbital Theory
sections.body:
Molecular orbital theory (Hund and Mulliken, 1932) says electrons in a molecule belong to the molecule as a whole and occupy molecular orbitals that spread over all the nuclei. Molecular orbitals are built by the linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO). Adding two 1s wave functions, ψA + ψB, gives a bonding orbital σ1s with more electron density between the nuclei and lower energy than the atomic orbitals; subtracting them, ψA − ψB, gives an antibonding orbital σ*1s with a node between the nuclei and higher energy. The bonding orbital is lowered by as much as the antibonding orbital is raised.

Conditions for combination: the atomic orbitals must have nearly the same energy, the same symmetry about the molecular axis, and must overlap as much as possible. So 2s combines with 2s, 2pz (taken along the axis) with 2pz to give σ2pz and σ*2pz, and 2px, 2py sideways to give the degenerate pairs π2px, π2py and π*2px, π*2py. Electrons fill the molecular orbitals by the aufbau principle, the Pauli principle and Hund's rule.

Energy order for O2 and F2: σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pz < (π2px = π2py) < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pz. For Li2, Be2, B2, C2 and N2 the σ2pz orbital lies above the π2p pair because of mixing between 2s and 2p, so the order is σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < (π2px = π2py) < σ2pz < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pz.

Bond order = ½(Nb − Na), the bonding electrons minus the antibonding electrons, halved. A positive bond order means the molecule can exist; zero or negative means it cannot. Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond. If every electron is paired the molecule is diamagnetic; any unpaired electron makes it paramagnetic. This is where MOT beats the Lewis picture: it predicts that O2, with two unpaired electrons in its π* orbitals, is paramagnetic, which experiment confirms.
sections.tip: For O2's paramagnetism name the orbitals: 'two unpaired electrons, one in each of the degenerate π*2px and π*2py orbitals, by Hund's rule'. 'O2 has unpaired electrons' alone is half marks.

sections.heading: 4.8 Bonding in Some Homonuclear Diatomic Molecules
sections.body:
H2 (2 electrons): σ1s2; bond order ½(2 − 0) = 1; diamagnetic; bond length 74 pm, bond enthalpy 435.8 kJ mol−1.

He2 (4): σ1s2 σ*1s2; bond order ½(2 − 2) = 0, so He2 does not exist. He2+ (3 electrons, σ1s2 σ*1s1) has bond order 0.5 and is known.

Li2 (6): σ1s2 σ*1s2 σ2s2, often written KK σ2s2; bond order 1; diamagnetic; exists in the vapour phase. Be2 (8): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2; bond order 0; does not exist. B2 (10): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2px1 π2py1; bond order 1; paramagnetic. C2 (12): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2px2 π2py2; bond order 2, both bonds are π; diamagnetic.

N2 (14): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2px2 π2py2 σ2pz2; bond order ½(10 − 4) = 3; diamagnetic; bond length 110 pm, bond enthalpy about 945 kJ mol−1, which is why N2 is so unreactive.

O2 (16): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 σ2pz2 π2px2 π2py2 π*2px1 π*2py1; bond order ½(10 − 6) = 2; paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons; 121 pm, 498 kJ mol−1. Remove an electron from π* and you get O2+, bond order 2.5, one unpaired electron, shorter bond. Add one for the superoxide O2−, bond order 1.5, one unpaired electron; add two for the peroxide O22−, bond order 1, diamagnetic. Stability and bond strength: O2+ > O2 > O2− > O22−; bond length runs the opposite way.

F2 (18): KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 σ2pz2 π2px2 π2py2 π*2px2 π*2py2; bond order 1; diamagnetic. Ne2 (20) fills σ*2pz as well, bond order 0, does not exist.
sections.tip: Learn the bond-order ladder for the O2 family (2.5, 2, 1.5, 1) and which members are paramagnetic (all except the peroxide). It is asked every year in some form.

sections.heading: 4.9 Hydrogen Bonding
sections.body:
When hydrogen is covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) the shared pair is pulled away from it, leaving the hydrogen with a large partial positive charge. That hydrogen is then attracted to the lone pair of an electronegative atom in a neighbouring molecule, or elsewhere in the same molecule. This attraction is a hydrogen bond, written as a dotted line: Hδ+–Fδ− ··· Hδ+–Fδ−. It is much weaker than a covalent bond (about 10 to 40 kJ mol−1) but stronger than van der Waals forces, and it needs F, O or N because only they are electronegative enough and small enough.

Intermolecular hydrogen bonding acts between molecules, of the same or different compounds: the zig-zag chains of HF, the network in water and ice, alcohols, carboxylic acids, and water–ethanol mixtures. Intramolecular hydrogen bonding acts within one molecule when the geometry allows a five- or six-membered ring, as in o-nitrophenol and salicylaldehyde.

Consequences the exam asks for: NH3, H2O and HF boil far higher than the other hydrides of their groups (water at 100 °C against −60 °C for H2S); water has a high viscosity, surface tension and specific heat; ice has an open hexagonal lattice in which each molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four neighbours, so it is less dense than liquid water and floats; o-nitrophenol is steam-volatile and lower boiling than p-nitrophenol, whose intermolecular hydrogen bonds hold the molecules together; ethanol and acetic acid dissolve in water because they hydrogen-bond with it; and the two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
sections.tip: For any boiling-point comparison among group 15, 16 or 17 hydrides, state that NH3, H2O and HF are the anomalies and say why in one line: intermolecular hydrogen bonding, absent in PH3, H2S and HCl.

key_terms.definition: Atoms gain, lose or share electrons so as to have eight electrons in the valence shell, the configuration of the nearest noble gas.
A diagram showing the bonding pairs (as lines or dot pairs) and lone pairs (as dots) of a molecule or ion around the atomic symbols.
The charge an atom would carry in a Lewis structure if all bonding electrons were shared equally: V − N − B/2. Used to choose the most reasonable structure.
The energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions; +788 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> for NaCl.
The energy required to break one mole of a particular bond in the gaseous state; for polyatomic molecules the mean of the successive bond dissociation enthalpies is used.
The number of bonds between two atoms in a Lewis structure, or in MOT half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons.
Describing a molecule as a hybrid of two or more canonical structures that differ only in the positions of electrons; the hybrid is more stable than any single structure.
A vector, μ = charge × distance, measuring the separation of charge in a bond or molecule; unit debye, 1 D = 3.33564 × 10<sup>−30</sup> C m.
Electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom repel one another and arrange themselves to minimise repulsion; the arrangement fixes the shape.
Mixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy on one atom to form an equal number of equivalent hybrid orbitals pointing in definite directions.
A covalent bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; cylindrically symmetric, allows free rotation.
A covalent bond formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals; electron cloud above and below the axis, weaker than a σ bond, no free rotation.
Orbitals formed by adding (ψ<sub>A</sub> + ψ<sub>B</sub>, lower energy, density between nuclei) and subtracting (ψ<sub>A</sub> − ψ<sub>B</sub>, higher energy, node between nuclei) atomic orbitals.
Attraction into a magnetic field shown by a species with one or more unpaired electrons, such as O<sub>2</sub>, B<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.
The attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on another F, O or N atom, in the same or a neighbouring molecule.

diagrams.title: VSEPR shapes of CH4, NH3 and H2O
diagrams.how_to_draw: Three sketches side by side. CH<sub>4</sub>: carbon at the centre of a tetrahedron, four C–H bonds, label 109.5°. NH<sub>3</sub>: nitrogen with three N–H bonds forming a pyramid and one lone pair drawn as a shaded lobe on top, label 107°. H<sub>2</sub>O: oxygen with two O–H bonds and two shaded lone-pair lobes, label 104.5°. Write the shape name under each (tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent) and use wedge and dash bonds to show depth.

diagrams.title: Potential energy curve for the formation of H2
diagrams.how_to_draw: Axes: internuclear distance on the x-axis, potential energy on the y-axis with zero at the level of two separated atoms. Draw the curve falling as the atoms approach, reaching a minimum, then rising steeply at short distances. Mark the minimum at 74 pm (bond length) and its depth as 435.8 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (bond enthalpy). Label the attractive and repulsive regions.

diagrams.title: Sigma and pi bonds in ethene
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two sp<sup>2</sup> carbons in a plane. Show one sp<sup>2</sup> lobe from each carbon overlapping head-on to form the C–C σ bond, the other two sp<sup>2</sup> lobes on each carbon forming σ bonds to hydrogens at about 120°. Draw the unhybridised p orbital on each carbon as two lobes above and below the plane, and shade the sideways overlap of the upper lobes and of the lower lobes as the single π bond. Label 'σ bond' and 'π bond' separately.

diagrams.title: Molecular orbital energy level diagram for O2
diagrams.how_to_draw: Atomic orbitals of the two oxygen atoms on the left and right (2s, and the three 2p), molecular orbitals in the middle in the order σ2s, σ*2s, σ2p<sub>z</sub>, the degenerate pair π2p<sub>x</sub> and π2p<sub>y</sub>, the degenerate pair π*2p<sub>x</sub> and π*2p<sub>y</sub>, and σ*2p<sub>z</sub> at the top. Fill 12 valence electrons with arrows, putting one unpaired arrow in each π* orbital. Write bond order = ½(8 − 4) = 2 for the valence shell and state paramagnetic. For N<sub>2</sub> swap σ2p<sub>z</sub> above the π2p pair and fill 10 electrons.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the formation of a chemical bond.
ncert_questions.a: A chemical bond is the attractive force that holds atoms together in a molecule or crystal. Atoms bond because the bonded state has lower energy than the separated atoms. By the Kössel–Lewis approach, an atom attains the stable octet of the nearest noble gas either by transferring electrons to another atom, giving oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction (ionic bond), or by sharing one or more electron pairs with another atom (covalent bond). The lowering of energy during transfer or sharing is what makes the bond form.

ncert_questions.q: Define the octet rule. Write its significance and limitations.
ncert_questions.a: Octet rule: atoms combine by transferring or sharing valence electrons so that each has eight electrons in its outermost shell. Significance: it explains the formation of ionic and covalent bonds and the valency of most main-group elements, and it lets us write Lewis structures. Limitations: (i) incomplete octet on the central atom in LiCl, BeH2, BF3 and AlCl3; (ii) odd-electron molecules such as NO and NO2 cannot satisfy it; (iii) expanded octet in PF5, SF6 and H2SO4, where the central atom has 10 or 12 electrons; (iv) it does not explain the shape of molecules or the relative stability of bonds; (v) noble gases, already with an octet, still form compounds such as XeF2 and KrF2.

ncert_questions.q: Although geometries of NH3 and H2O molecules are distorted tetrahedral, bond angle in water is less than that of ammonia. Discuss.
ncert_questions.a: Both N and O are sp3 hybridised with four electron pairs, so the parent geometry is tetrahedral. NH3 has three bond pairs and one lone pair; H2O has two bond pairs and two lone pairs. A lone pair is held by one nucleus only and spreads out more, so lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. In NH3 one lone pair pushes the three bond pairs together, reducing the angle from 109.5° to 107°. In H2O the two lone pairs repel each other strongly and also both bond pairs, so the compression is greater and the angle falls to 104.5°.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the important aspects of resonance with reference to the CO3 2- ion.
ncert_questions.a: A single Lewis structure of CO32− has one C=O double bond and two C–O single bonds, which would make one bond shorter than the other two. Experiment shows all three C–O bonds equal, intermediate between single and double. So the ion is a resonance hybrid of three canonical structures in which the double bond sits on each oxygen in turn. Points to state: the canonical structures differ only in electron positions, not atom positions; none of them exists on its own, only the hybrid is real; the hybrid has lower energy than any canonical form (resonance stabilisation); each C–O bond order is 4/3; the ion is trigonal planar.

ncert_questions.q: Write the resonance structures for SO3, NO2 and NO3-.
ncert_questions.a: SO3: S at the centre bonded to three O atoms in a plane; draw one S=O double bond and two S–O single bonds, and repeat with the double bond on each of the other two oxygens, giving three equivalent structures. NO2: N at the centre with one N=O and one N–O bond and the odd electron on N; the second structure swaps which oxygen carries the double bond, so two equivalent structures. NO3−: N bonded to three O atoms, one N=O double bond and two N–O− single bonds; rotating the double bond gives three equivalent structures, all N–O bonds equal, trigonal planar. In each case the real molecule is the hybrid and the bonds are identical.

ncert_questions.q: Write the significance/applications of dipole moment.
ncert_questions.a: (i) It tells polar from non-polar molecules: μ = 0 for H2, CO2, BF3; μ > 0 for HCl, H2O, NH3. (ii) It indicates shape: a triatomic AB2 molecule with zero dipole moment is linear (CO2, BeCl2), one with a net dipole is bent (H2O, SO2). (iii) It gives the percentage ionic character of a bond by comparing the observed dipole moment with the value expected for complete charge transfer. (iv) It distinguishes cis and trans isomers, because the cis isomer usually has the higher dipole moment.

ncert_questions.q: Apart from tetrahedral geometry, another possible geometry for CH4 is square planar with the four H atoms at the corners of a square and the C atom at its centre. Explain why CH4 is not square planar.
ncert_questions.a: Carbon in CH4 is sp3 hybridised, and four equivalent electron pairs keep farthest apart in a tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5°. A square planar arrangement would force the bond pairs to 90°, so the repulsion between them would be greater and the energy higher. Also, a square planar shape needs dsp2 hybridisation, and carbon has no d orbitals in its valence shell. The tetrahedral shape is therefore the one of minimum energy.

ncert_questions.q: Explain why BeH2 molecule has a zero dipole moment although the Be–H bonds are polar.
ncert_questions.a: Beryllium has no lone pair and forms two bond pairs, so by VSEPR (and sp hybridisation) BeH2 is linear, H–Be–H with a 180° angle. Each Be–H bond is polar because H is more electronegative than Be, giving a bond dipole from Be towards each H. The two bond dipoles are equal in magnitude and point in exactly opposite directions, so their vector sum is zero. The molecule has no net dipole moment; the cancellation comes from the geometry, not from the bonds being non-polar.

ncert_questions.q: Which out of NH3 and NF3 has higher dipole moment and why?
ncert_questions.a: NH3 (1.47 D) has the higher dipole moment; NF3 has only 0.24 D. Both are trigonal pyramidal with one lone pair on nitrogen. In NH3, N is more electronegative than H, so the three N–H bond dipoles point towards N, in the same direction as the lone-pair moment, and they add. In NF3, F is more electronegative than N, so the N–F bond dipoles point away from N towards the fluorines, opposite to the lone-pair moment, and they partly cancel. The net dipole of NF3 is therefore much smaller.

ncert_questions.q: Compare the relative stability of the following species and indicate their magnetic properties: O2, O2+, O2- (superoxide), O2 2- (peroxide).
ncert_questions.a: Valence configurations after KK σ2s2 σ*2s2 σ2pz2 π2px2 π2py2: O2+ (15 electrons) has π*2p1, bond order ½(10 − 5) = 2.5, one unpaired electron, paramagnetic. O2 (16) has π*2px1 π*2py1, bond order ½(10 − 6) = 2, two unpaired electrons, paramagnetic. O2− (17) has π*2px2 π*2py1, bond order ½(10 − 7) = 1.5, one unpaired electron, paramagnetic. O22− (18) has π*2px2 π*2py2, bond order ½(10 − 8) = 1, all paired, diamagnetic. Stability follows bond order: O2+ > O2 > O2− > O22−.

ncert_questions.q: Define hydrogen bond. Is it weaker or stronger than the van der Waals forces?
ncert_questions.a: A hydrogen bond is the attractive force between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom of the same or a neighbouring molecule, shown as a dotted line, for example H–F ··· H–F. It arises because the H atom carries a large partial positive charge. A hydrogen bond (roughly 10 to 40 kJ mol−1) is stronger than van der Waals forces but much weaker than a covalent bond.

ncert_questions.q: What is meant by the term bond order? Calculate the bond order of: N2, O2, O2+ and O2-.
ncert_questions.a: Bond order is half the difference between the number of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals, BO = ½(Nb − Na). N2 (14 electrons): 10 bonding, 4 antibonding, BO = ½(10 − 4) = 3. O2 (16): 10 bonding, 6 antibonding, BO = ½(10 − 6) = 2. O2+ (15): 10 bonding, 5 antibonding, BO = ½(10 − 5) = 2.5. O2− (17): 10 bonding, 7 antibonding, BO = ½(10 − 7) = 1.5.

pyq.q: The hybridisation of phosphorus in PCl<sub>5</sub> is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: P has five bond pairs and no lone pair, steric number 5, so sp<sup>3</sup>d and a trigonal bipyramidal shape.

pyq.q: Which of the following species is diamagnetic?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: N<sub>2</sub> has all electrons paired (bond order 3). O<sub>2</sub> has two unpaired electrons and O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> one each, all in π* orbitals.

pyq.q: The shape of ClF<sub>3</sub> according to VSEPR theory is:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Cl has three bond pairs and two lone pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d); the lone pairs take two equatorial positions of the trigonal bipyramid, leaving a T-shaped molecule.

pyq.q: Which pair of species is isoelectronic and has the same bond order?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: CO and N<sub>2</sub> both have 14 electrons and bond order 3; O<sub>2</sub> has 16 electrons and bond order 2, NO has 15 and bond order 2.5.

pyq.q: Among NH<sub>3</sub>, PH<sub>3</sub> and AsH<sub>3</sub> the bond angle is largest in:
options: AsH<sub>3</sub>, because As is the largest atom
NH<sub>3</sub>, because N is the most electronegative so the bond pairs lie closest to it and repel one another most
All three have the same bond angle
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Down the group the central atom becomes less electronegative and larger, the bond pairs move away from it, bp–bp repulsion falls and the angle drops: NH<sub>3</sub> 107°, PH<sub>3</sub> about 94°, AsH<sub>3</sub> about 92°.

pyq.q: The correct order of decreasing bond order is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Electrons added to O<sub>2</sub> go into antibonding π* orbitals and lower the bond order; removing one raises it: 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Ionic solids conduct electricity in the molten state but not in the solid state. Reason (R): In the solid state the ions are held rigidly in the lattice; on melting they become free to move.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Conduction needs mobile ions, which exist only in the melt or in solution, so R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Both O–O bond lengths in ozone are equal, 128 pm, between a single and a double bond. Reason (R): Ozone is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent canonical structures.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The delocalised π electrons of the hybrid give both bonds a bond order of 1.5 and hence equal, intermediate length; R is the exact reason for A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The bond angle in H<sub>2</sub>O (104.5°) is smaller than in NH<sub>3</sub> (107°). Reason (R): H<sub>2</sub>O has two lone pairs on the central atom and NH<sub>3</sub> one, and lone pair–lone pair repulsion is stronger than lone pair–bond pair repulsion.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both statements are correct and R is the VSEPR reasoning that produces the smaller angle in water.

pyq.q: Draw the Lewis structure of CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> and calculate the formal charge on each atom.
pyq.answer: 24 valence electrons (4 + 18 + 2). C at the centre with one C=O double bond and two C–O single bonds; each single-bonded O carries three lone pairs, the double-bonded O two. Formal charges: C = 4 − 0 − 8/2 = 0; double-bonded O = 6 − 4 − 4/2 = 0; each single-bonded O = 6 − 6 − 2/2 = −1. Total −2, matching the charge on the ion.

pyq.q: State the hybridisation and shape of XeF<sub>4</sub>. Give reason.
pyq.answer: Xe has eight valence electrons; four form Xe–F bond pairs and the other four make two lone pairs, so six electron pairs, sp3d2 hybridisation, octahedral electron-pair geometry. The two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) positions to minimise lp–lp repulsion, leaving the four F atoms in one plane: square planar shape, 90° F–Xe–F angles.

pyq.q: Define lattice enthalpy. Why is the lattice enthalpy of MgO much higher than that of NaCl?
pyq.answer: Lattice enthalpy is the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions (NaCl: +788 kJ mol−1). It increases with the charge on the ions and decreases with their size. MgO contains Mg2+ and O2−, doubly charged and smaller than Na+ and Cl−, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is far stronger and the lattice enthalpy is much larger (about 3800 kJ mol−1).

pyq.q: Define bond order. Calculate it for He<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and comment on whether the ion can exist.
pyq.answer: Bond order = ½(number of electrons in bonding MOs − number in antibonding MOs). He2+ has three electrons: σ1s2 σ*1s1. Bond order = ½(2 − 1) = 0.5. Because the bond order is positive the ion can exist, though the bond is weak; neutral He2, with bond order 0, cannot.

pyq.q: Explain the formation of the H<sub>2</sub> molecule on the basis of valence bond theory, with an energy diagram.
pyq.answer: Consider two hydrogen atoms A and B, each with one electron in a 1s orbital, initially far apart with no interaction. As they approach, attractive forces arise between nucleus A and electron B and between nucleus B and electron A, and repulsive forces between the two electrons and between the two nuclei. Attraction outweighs repulsion, so the potential energy falls as the atoms come closer. At an internuclear distance of 74 pm the energy is minimum: the 1s orbitals overlap, the electron pair is shared, and 435.8 kJ mol−1 is released (the bond enthalpy). If the atoms come still closer, nuclear repulsion dominates and the energy rises sharply. Diagram: potential energy against internuclear distance, a curve dipping to a minimum at 74 pm, depth 435.8 kJ mol−1, rising steeply to the left.

pyq.q: Is there any change in the hybridisation of the central atoms in the following reactions? (a) AlCl<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sup>−</sup> → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (b) BF<sub>3</sub> + NH<sub>3</sub> → F<sub>3</sub>B·NH<sub>3</sub>
pyq.answer: (a) In AlCl3 aluminium has three bond pairs and no lone pair: sp2, trigonal planar. Cl− donates a lone pair into the empty p orbital of Al, giving four bond pairs in AlCl4−: sp3, tetrahedral. So Al changes from sp2 to sp3. (b) In BF3 boron is sp2 (three bond pairs, trigonal planar). Nitrogen in NH3 is sp3 (three bond pairs, one lone pair). When N donates its lone pair to the empty p orbital of B, boron acquires four bond pairs and becomes sp3, tetrahedral; nitrogen still has four electron pairs, all now bond pairs, and stays sp3. So B changes from sp2 to sp3; N does not change.

pyq.q: State Fajans' rule. Why is LiCl more covalent than NaCl?
pyq.answer: Fajans' rule: the covalent character of an ionic bond increases when the cation is small and highly charged (high polarising power) and the anion is large and easily deformable (high polarisability). The cation distorts the electron cloud of the anion towards itself, pulling electron density into the region between the nuclei, so the bond acquires covalent character. Li+ and Na+ carry the same charge, but Li+ is much smaller, so its charge density and polarising power are higher. Li+ polarises the Cl− ion more than Na+ does, which is why LiCl has more covalent character than NaCl, dissolves in organic solvents such as ethanol, and has the lower melting point.

pyq.q: Distinguish between a sigma bond and a pi bond.
pyq.answer: (i) Overlap: a σ bond forms by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis (s–s, s–p or p–p end to end); a π bond forms by sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals perpendicular to the axis. (ii) Electron cloud: σ is cylindrically symmetric about the axis; π has its density above and below the axis with a nodal plane through the nuclei. (iii) Strength: σ is stronger because head-on overlap is greater. (iv) Rotation: free rotation is possible about a σ bond but not about a π bond, since rotation would break the sideways overlap. (v) Occurrence: a σ bond can exist alone; a π bond forms only in addition to a σ bond, as in C=C and C≡C.

pyq.q: Describe the hybridisation in PCl<sub>5</sub> and draw its shape. Why are the axial bonds longer than the equatorial bonds?
pyq.answer: Ground-state P is 3s23p3. One 3s electron is promoted to a 3d orbital, giving 3s13p33d1, and the five half-filled orbitals mix to form five sp3d hybrid orbitals directed to the corners of a trigonal bipyramid. Each overlaps with a half-filled 3p orbital of chlorine to form a P–Cl σ bond. Shape: three Cl atoms in an equatorial plane at 120° to one another, and two Cl atoms axial, one above and one below the plane, each at 90° to the equatorial bonds. (Draw the trigonal bipyramid with P at the centre, label the 120° and 90° angles, and mark axial and equatorial bonds.) Each axial bond pair experiences three repulsions at 90° from the equatorial pairs, whereas each equatorial pair experiences only two 90° repulsions from the axial pairs, the other two equatorial pairs being at 120°. Since 90° repulsions are much stronger than 120° repulsions, the axial bond pairs are pushed slightly farther from the nucleus, so the axial P–Cl bonds (240 pm) are longer and weaker than the equatorial ones (202 pm). This is also why PCl5 is reactive and loses the axial chlorines easily.

pyq.q: Using molecular orbital theory compare N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>: write their electronic configurations, calculate bond orders, and predict bond length, bond strength and magnetic behaviour.
pyq.answer: N2 (14 electrons; π2p lies below σ2pz): σ1s2 σ*1s2 σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2px2 π2py2 σ2pz2. Nb = 10, Na = 4, bond order = ½(10 − 4) = 3, a triple bond. All electrons paired: diamagnetic. Short bond (110 pm) and very high bond enthalpy (about 945 kJ mol−1), so N2 is inert. O2 (16 electrons; σ2pz lies below π2p): σ1s2 σ*1s2 σ2s2 σ*2s2 σ2pz2 π2px2 π2py2 π*2px1 π*2py1. Nb = 10, Na = 6, bond order = ½(10 − 6) = 2, a double bond. The last two electrons enter the degenerate π*2px and π*2py orbitals singly by Hund's rule, so O2 has two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic, which the Lewis structure O=O cannot explain. Bond length 121 pm, bond enthalpy 498 kJ mol−1. Summary: N2 has the higher bond order, the shorter and stronger bond and is diamagnetic; O2 has the lower bond order, a longer and weaker bond and is paramagnetic. Draw the two MO energy diagrams with arrows to earn the diagram marks.

pyq.q: Explain the hybridisation of carbon in ethane, ethene and ethyne. State the number of sigma and pi bonds in each and the C–C bond length trend.
pyq.answer: Ethane, H3C–CH3: each carbon is sp3 hybridised (one 2s + three 2p → four orbitals at 109.5°). One sp3 orbital of each carbon overlaps head-on with one of the other to give the C–C σ bond; the remaining three on each carbon overlap with 1s orbitals of hydrogen to give six C–H σ bonds. Total 7 σ, 0 π; free rotation about C–C; C–C 154 pm. Ethene, H2C=CH2: each carbon is sp2 hybridised (one 2s + two 2p → three coplanar orbitals at 120°). One sp2 orbital forms the C–C σ bond and the other two form C–H σ bonds; the unhybridised 2p orbital on each carbon, perpendicular to the plane, overlaps sideways with the other to give one π bond. Total 5 σ + 1 π; planar; C=C 134 pm. Ethyne, HC≡CH: each carbon is sp hybridised (one 2s + one 2p → two orbitals at 180°). One sp orbital forms the C–C σ bond and the other a C–H σ bond; the two remaining 2p orbitals on each carbon, mutually perpendicular, overlap sideways with those on the other carbon to give two π bonds. Total 3 σ + 2 π; linear; C≡C 120 pm. The bond length falls from ethane to ethyne as the bond order rises from 1 to 3 and the s character of the hybrid rises from 25% to 50%.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Water boils at 100 °C while hydrogen sulfide, whose molecule is heavier, boils at about −60 °C. Ice has an open hexagonal structure and floats on liquid water, which lets aquatic life survive the winter under a frozen surface.
(i) Name the intermolecular force responsible for the high boiling point of water.
(ii) Why does H2S not show a similarly high boiling point?
(iii) Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
(iv) Name one other property of water that this force affects.
pyq.answer:
(i) Intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the H of one water molecule and a lone pair on the O of a neighbour.
(ii) Sulfur is larger and much less electronegative than oxygen, so the S–H bond is barely polar and H2S molecules cannot hydrogen-bond; only weak van der Waals forces hold them together, so the boiling point is low despite the higher molar mass.
(iii) In ice every water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four neighbours in a rigid open hexagonal lattice with empty space inside the rings. On melting some hydrogen bonds break, the structure partly collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice.
(iv) High viscosity, high surface tension or high specific heat capacity; also its ability to dissolve ethanol, sugars and other hydrogen-bonding solutes.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
VSEPR theory predicts the shape of a molecule from the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom. Consider BF3, NH3, SF4 and XeF2.
(i) State the hybridisation and shape of BF3.
(ii) State the hybridisation and shape of NH3 and explain why its bond angle is less than 109.5°.
(iii) State the hybridisation and shape of SF4.
(iv) State the hybridisation and shape of XeF2 and say where its lone pairs lie.
pyq.answer:
(i) B: three bond pairs, no lone pair; sp2; trigonal planar, 120°.
(ii) N: three bond pairs and one lone pair; sp3; trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly than they repel one another (lp–bp > bp–bp), compressing the H–N–H angle to 107°.
(iii) S: four bond pairs and one lone pair; sp3d; see-saw, with the lone pair in an equatorial position of the trigonal bipyramid.
(iv) Xe: two bond pairs and three lone pairs; sp3d; linear. All three lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions of the trigonal bipyramid, so the two F atoms are axial, 180° apart.

practice_mcq.q: The number of lone pairs on the central atom in SF<sub>6</sub> is:
practice_mcq.explanation: All six valence electrons of S are used in S–F bonds (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), so there is no lone pair and the shape is a regular octahedron.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following has the shortest bond length?
practice_mcq.explanation: N<sub>2</sub> has bond order 3; N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and N<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> have 2.5 and N<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup> has 2, so N<sub>2</sub> has the shortest bond.

practice_mcq.q: The hybridisation of carbon in the carbonate ion is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Carbon forms three σ bonds and has no lone pair: steric number 3, sp<sup>2</sup>, trigonal planar.

practice_mcq.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though its bonds are polar?
practice_mcq.explanation: CO<sub>2</sub> is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles cancel; the other three are bent or pyramidal and have a net dipole.

practice_mcq.q: According to MOT the bond order of the peroxide ion O<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup> is:
practice_mcq.explanation: 18 electrons, 10 bonding and 8 antibonding: ½(10 − 8) = 1, the same as F<sub>2</sub>.

practice_mcq.q: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding is present in:
practice_mcq.explanation: In o-nitrophenol the O–H and the adjacent NO<sub>2</sub> group are close enough to hydrogen-bond within the same molecule through a six-membered ring; the others show intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

practice_mcq.q: A central atom with four bond pairs and two lone pairs gives the shape:
practice_mcq.explanation: Six pairs give an octahedral arrangement; the two lone pairs go opposite each other, leaving four atoms in a square plane, as in XeF<sub>4</sub>.

practice_mcq.q: Which species does not exist according to molecular orbital theory?
practice_mcq.explanation: He<sub>2</sub> is σ1s<sup>2</sup> σ*1s<sup>2</sup>, bond order 0. H<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (0.5), Li<sub>2</sub> (1) and B<sub>2</sub> (1) all have positive bond order.

practice_mcq.q: A π bond is formed by:
options: Head-on overlap along the internuclear axis
Sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals
practice_mcq.explanation: Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals perpendicular to the axis gives electron density above and below the axis, the π bond.

practice_mcq.q: According to Fajans' rule, covalent character in an ionic bond is favoured by:
options: A large cation and a small anion
A small, highly charged cation and a large, polarisable anion
Ions of equal size and charge
A large, highly charged cation and a small anion
practice_mcq.explanation: A small, highly charged cation has high polarising power and a large anion is easily polarised, so electron density is pulled between the nuclei.

practice_mcq.q: The bond order of the superoxide ion O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is:
practice_mcq.explanation: 17 electrons: 10 bonding, 7 antibonding, bond order ½(10 − 7) = 1.5, with one unpaired electron.

practice_mcq.q: Which central atom is sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridised?
practice_mcq.explanation: S in SF<sub>6</sub> has six bond pairs and no lone pair, steric number 6, sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, octahedral.

practice_mcq.q: In the Lewis structure of BF<sub>3</sub>, boron has:
practice_mcq.explanation: Boron has three valence electrons and forms three single bonds, so it has six electrons around it, an incomplete octet.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about resonance structures is correct?
options: They are separate molecules in rapid equilibrium
They differ in the positions of atoms
The real molecule is a hybrid of all of them and is more stable than any one
Only one of them is real at any instant
practice_mcq.explanation: Canonical structures are imaginary; only the hybrid, with delocalised electrons and lower energy, exists.

practice_mcq.q: The number of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals of N<sub>2</sub> is respectively:
practice_mcq.explanation: N<sub>2</sub> has 14 electrons, 10 in bonding and 4 in antibonding orbitals, giving bond order ½(10 − 4) = 3.

common_mistakes: Naming the electron-pair geometry as the shape: NH3 is trigonal pyramidal, not tetrahedral; the examiner wants both words in the right places.
Forgetting the lone pairs on the central atom when applying VSEPR, which turns bent H2O into 'linear' and T-shaped ClF3 into 'trigonal planar'.
Using the N2 energy order (π2p below σ2pz) for O2 and F2, or the other way round; for the bond order it does not matter, but the written configuration is marked.
Explaining O2's paramagnetism with 'it has a double bond' instead of the two unpaired electrons in the degenerate π*2p orbitals.
Calling CO2 or BF3 polar because their bonds are polar; the net dipole is a vector sum and cancels in a symmetric shape.
Treating resonance structures as real molecules that interconvert; they are drawings, only the hybrid exists.
Writing lattice enthalpy as a negative number with the NCERT definition, which is the energy required to break the lattice and is positive.
Saying all five P–Cl bonds in PCl5 are identical; the axial bonds are longer, and the reason (three 90° repulsions against two) is a marking point.
strategy:
Build the chapter in the order NCERT does, because each idea sits on the one before it. Start with Lewis structures and formal charge until you can draw O3, CO32−, NO3−, SO2 and ClO4− quickly and check the charges add up. Then memorise the VSEPR table as pairs of numbers (bond pairs, lone pairs) with the shape, the angle and one example each; twelve entries cover every question the school paper asks. Learn the CH4, NH3, H2O angle argument word for word.

Hybridisation is a five-mark question in most school finals: practise writing ethane, ethene and ethyne with the promotion step, the number of hybrid orbitals, the σ and π counts and the bond lengths, and draw the orbital picture for ethene once a day for a week. For MOT, write both energy orders from memory, then fill H2 to Ne2 and the O2 family, computing bond order and magnetic nature each time; this is the most repeated question across school exams, JEE and NEET. Finish with hydrogen bonding, which is a ready-made two- or three-mark answer about boiling points and ice.

In the exam show the arithmetic: the formal-charge sum, the ½(Nb − Na) step, the steric-number count. Partial credit lives in those lines. Allocate about a quarter of your revision time for this chapter to diagrams, because the shape, the ethene overlap picture and the MO diagram each carry a mark on their own.
revision_checklist: Can draw the Lewis structure of any simple molecule or ion and check it with formal charges (O3, CO3 2-, NO3-, SO2, ClO4-).
Can list the limitations of the octet rule with one example each.
Can state the NCERT definition of lattice enthalpy with its sign and the three factors favouring ionic bonding.
Can define bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy (mean bond enthalpy) and bond order, and relate bond order to length and enthalpy.
Can explain resonance with ozone and carbonate, including the 128 pm bond-length argument.
Can explain zero dipole moment in CO2, BF3 and BeH2 and the NH3 > NF3 comparison.
Knows the VSEPR shape, angle and lone-pair count for BeCl2, BF3, CH4, NH3, H2O, PCl5, SF4, ClF3, XeF2, SF6, BrF5, XeF4.
Can describe the formation of H2 by VBT with the energy curve (74 pm, 435.8 kJ/mol).
Can list five differences between sigma and pi bonds.
Can write the hybridisation, orbital picture and sigma/pi count for ethane, ethene and ethyne.
Can write both MO energy orders and the configuration, bond order and magnetism of H2, He2, Li2, N2, O2, O2+, O2-, O2 2-, F2.
Can explain why O2 is paramagnetic and why He2 and Be2 do not exist.
Can define hydrogen bonding, give one intermolecular and one intramolecular example, and explain the H2O vs H2S boiling points and why ice floats.
